source.title: LSTM Hyperparameters optimization with Hparam parameters for Bitcoin Price Prediction

record.tranche_reason: Reports its own train and test error results for LSTM hyperparameter changes on Bitcoin time-series forecasting, a setting outside the claim versions' specified classification tasks.
record.gate_note: The study reports train and test MSE for Bitcoin price prediction. Those results bear on training-to-test error differences in a related forecasting setting, but none of the claim versions' specified behaviors or settings is tested. Reported values for multiple hyperparameter settings are recorded below; cited studies' results are not included.
record.test_reason: The study measures Bitcoin forecasting MSE for recurrent LSTMs. Its optimizer, batch-size and dropout comparisons concern regression rather than the image classifiers, language benchmarks or classifier architectures named in V4–V6. It does not measure the behaviors in V1–V3 or V7–V8. Related forecasting results and citations to original sources do not constitute a test of these versions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate: the authors conclude that hyperparameter combinations affect Bitcoin forecasting MSE, report different preferred learning-rate and dropout settings for daily and hourly data, and recommend hourly data because its reported test MSE is lower. These are the authors' interpretations; the reported comparisons do not establish universal preferences.
record.recipe_differences: LSTM Bitcoin time-series regression with manually varied hyperparameters; no random-label classification, image or language benchmark, or generalization-measure experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported train/test MSE varies with go-backward, activation, optimizer, learning rate, batch size, number of layers, epoch, dropout, and dataset interval. The paper states daily and hourly data favor different learning-rate and dropout settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Forward versus backward processing changes daily Bitcoin forecasting MSE; forward processing has lower test MSE at both reported epoch counts.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Processing direction can affect LSTM forecasting error.

fits_no_version.finding: At 100 epochs, Adam with tanh has test MSE 0.000667 versus SGD with tanh at 0.328543; both training and test performance differ substantially.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Optimizer and activation choices affect LSTM Bitcoin regression performance at a fixed training budget.

fits_no_version.finding: Increasing Adam training to 1000 epochs improves sigmoid and softmax results relative to their 100-epoch values, but their test MSE remains above tanh's 100-epoch result.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Additional training does not eliminate activation-dependent forecasting differences in these LSTM experiments.

fits_no_version.finding: Table 4 reports lower daily test MSE as batch size increases from 32 to 128. Table 6 reports that dropout 0.1 lowers daily test MSE but slightly raises hourly test MSE.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Batch-size and dropout effects in LSTM Bitcoin regression depend on the dataset and training configuration.

record.peer_reviewed: Sakarya University Journal of Computer and Information Sciences
record.problems: The study is a Bitcoin time-series forecasting regression, not the classification settings specified by the claim versions. It reports point MSE values without uncertainty estimates. Some table/result descriptions are internally inconsistent: Table 3 is introduced as the learning-rate effect but includes repeated values, and the paper's discussion of layers and batch size is not uniformly aligned with the tabulated results.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2's remaining entries are included through R56. Other hyperparameter rows are not extracted because the 60-row limit is reached; the study's remaining directly reported settings include the learning-rate values in Table 3, batch-size comparison in Table 4, layer comparison in Table 5, dropout comparison in Table 6, and hourly/daily top-ten combinations in Tables 7 and 8. These settings are also outside the specified claim-version tasks.

untested.parts: Random-label memorization, natural-label held-out accuracy and chance-level random-label generalization.
Width increases beyond zero training error in converged one-hidden-layer ReLU networks.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and the contribution of local connectivity.
Adaptive versus SGD generalization on image-classification or language benchmarks under the specified tuning regimes.
Large-batch penalties and recipe adaptations in image classifiers or language models under fixed epoch budgets.
Dropout effects in fully connected or convolutional classifiers, including small-data, underfitting and augmentation conditions.
Magnitude-aware sharpness, generalization-gap correlations and comparisons with other measures.
Removing examples selected by label memorization versus removing random examples.

record.verdict_notes: All 60 extracted MSE values match the supplied text. Their existing none links and cannot_determine states are appropriate relative to V1–V8. Tables 3–8 are already declared in rows_left_out, so they are not missing entries. Section 4.4 additionally reports SGD at 1000 epochs with training MSE 0.000020 and test MSE 0.000859; this unrecorded forecasting result also fits no version. Table 1's claim that backward processing improves training MSE holds at 100 epochs but not at 10 epochs. Top-ten configurations in Tables 7–8 are selected results and do not isolate individual hyperparameter effects.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label fitting and natural-label generalization coexistence.
Width sweeps beyond interpolation on MNIST or downsampled CIFAR-10.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local connectivity.
Adaptive optimizer comparisons on image-classification or language benchmarks.
Large-batch effects under fixed epoch budgets on image-classification or language tasks.
Dropout effects in fully connected or convolutional classifiers.
Magnitude-aware sharpness and other generalization measures.
Removing memorized training examples and measuring test accuracy.
